finding.claim: Authorization decisions use g.user, which is never set in this repository. If the value that populates g.user is client-controlled, any caller can impersonate a note owner or sharer and read, modify, or share notes. Conditional and unverified.
finding.source: g.user, read at notes.py:28, :35, and :44. Nothing in the repo assigns it. A grep for g.user, before_request, login, session, token, and Authorization matched only those three read sites.
finding.sink: Protected operations: note read (notes.py:29, jsonify(n)), note body write (notes.py:37), and share-list append (notes.py:45).

trace.note: can_view compares note owner and shared list to the user value
require_view aborts 403 when the check fails

finding.guards_checked: No authentication, session, or before_request hook exists in the repo. If g.user is never set, every request raises AttributeError and returns 500, which fails closed. Owner-only edit and share rules (notes.py:17, :44) are correct as written. The source of g.user is in code not provided, so this cannot be confirmed or ruled out.

verdict.guard_found: require_view at notes.py:11-13 aborts 403 when can_view (notes.py:8) fails, and its result is not discarded because abort raises. can_edit at notes.py:16-17 is checked by the if-abort at notes.py:35-36, and require_edit at notes.py:20-22 aborts on failure and is called as a bare statement at notes.py:44 but still enforces the check. Owner-only edit and share rules hold as written. No in-repo code sets g.user, so an unset g.user raises AttributeError (500), which fails closed.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code (notes.py:8, 12-13, 17, 21-22, 28, 35-37, 44-45), and the authorization checks abort correctly, but whether g.user is client-controlled depends on code outside this repository (the finding itself calls the claim conditional), so the exploitability of the impersonation path cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.claim: Unknown note IDs raise an unhandled KeyError (500) before any authorization check, while existing but unauthorized IDs return 403. This lets a caller distinguish existing note IDs. Low severity; matters only if IDs are guessable.
finding.source: URL segment <nid> on the read, write, and share routes (notes.py:25, :32, :41).
finding.sink: Existence of entries in the NOTES dict (notes.py:27, :34, :43).

trace.note: read route accepts <nid> from the URL
NOTES[nid] lookup with no membership check; KeyError on unknown ID
authorization runs only after the lookup succeeds
403 returned for known IDs the caller cannot view

finding.guards_checked: No existence check, 404 handler, or error handler in the file. Write and share routes (:34, :43) follow the same pattern.

verdict.guard_found: none. notes.py:27, :34, :43 index NOTES[nid] with no membership check and no try/except; no 404 or error handler exists in notes.py (the only file in the directory); require_view/can_edit checks at :28, :35, :44 run only after the lookup, and abort(403) at :13 is reached only for IDs that exist.
verdict.reason: At notes.py:27 an unknown nid raises KeyError before require_view at notes.py:28 runs, while a known note the caller cannot view gets abort(403) at notes.py:13, so the 500-versus-403 difference is a valid existence oracle. The trace is accurate; the only remaining uncertainty is how g.user is set, since no auth middleware is in the directory, so the attacker's required privilege is not established, but the leak itself is real and the finding's low severity is consistent with it.
